examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Maclaurin Expansion of a Sum of Functions Using Standard Maclaurin Expansions
examples.problem: Find the first four non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of $e^x+\sin(2x).$
examples.worked_solution:
The Maclaurin series for $e^x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & =1+x+\frac{1}{2!}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3!}\,{x}^{3}+⋯ \\  & =1+x+\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{6}\,{x}^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

The Maclaurin series for $\sin{x}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x=x-\frac{1}{3!}{x}^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Replacing $x$ with $2x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & =2x-\frac{1}{3!}(2x)^{3}+⋯ \\  & =2x-\frac{4}{3}\,{x}^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the expansions for $e^{x}$ and $\sin(2x)$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & =(1+x+\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{6}\,{x}^{3}+⋯)+(2x-\frac{4}{3}\,{x}^{3}+⋯) \\  & =1+(1+2)x+\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}+(\frac{1}{6}-\frac{4}{3}){x}^{3}+⋯ \\  & =1+3x+\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}-\frac{7}{6}\,{x}^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

This series has an infinite radius of convergence because the series expansions for $e^x$ and $\sin x$ both have an infinite radius of convergence.

feedback.problem: Find the first four non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of $\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The standard Maclaurin expansion for $\frac{1}{1-x}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1-x} & =1+x+{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

Replacing $x$ with $-4{x}^{2}$ in the above expansion and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}} & =1+(-4{x}^{2})+{(-4{x}^{2})}^{2}+{(-4{x}^{2})}^{3}+⋯ \\  & =1-4{x}^{2}+16{x}^{4}-64{x}^{6}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get an expansion for $\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}},$ we multiply the above expansion by $2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}} & =2(1-4{x}^{2}+16{x}^{4}-64{x}^{6}+⋯) \\  & =2-8{x}^{2}+32{x}^{4}-128{x}^{6}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$
